title: Romania's Orphans and Foster Care
text:
After the fall of the Ceausescu regime in 1989, the world learned that tens of thousands of Romanian children were living in large, understaffed orphanages. In 2000, with the Romanian government's agreement, a team of American researchers led by Charles Nelson, Charles Zeanah and Nathan Fox began the Bucharest Early Intervention Project.

They assessed 136 young children living in Bucharest institutions. Because Romania had almost no foster care at the time, the team built a foster care network and randomly assigned half of the children to move into foster families while the other half received the usual care, which mostly meant staying in the institution. A group of children who had never been institutionalized served as a further comparison.

In 2007 the team reported in Science that, by age four and a half, the children placed in foster families had higher IQ scores than those who stayed. The timing mattered: children who moved before about two years of age gained the most, while later placements helped less.

The study raised hard ethical questions, which the team addressed by never blocking adoption or family placement and by handing the foster network over to local authorities. Its results helped push Romania and other countries away from institutional care for young children.
lesson: For a young child, a family is not a luxury. When a child is in trouble, acting early does far more good than acting late.
people: Charles Nelson, Charles Zeanah, Nathan Fox and colleagues
source: Nelson, C. A., Zeanah, C. H., Fox, N. A., Marshall, P. J., Smyke, A. T., and Guthrie, D. (2007). Cognitive recovery in socially deprived young children: The Bucharest Early Intervention Project. Science, 318(5858), 1937-1940.
